139	# Committing and pushing
140	
141	**scratch**
142	: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.
143	
144	Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.
145	
146	## What to commit
147	
148	- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
149	- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
150	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
151	- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
152	- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
153	- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
154	- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.
155	
156	## How to commit
157	
158	Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:
159	
160	    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
161	
162	- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
163	- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
164	- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
165	- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
166	- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
167	- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:
168	
169	      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
170	      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
171	
172	  If your brief gives another session line, use it.
173	
174	## Pushing
175	
176	Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.
177	
178	- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
179	- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
180	  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
181	  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
182	  3. If it lists only your commits, push three times, in this order:
183	
184	         git push origin main
185	         git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8
186	         git push origin main:blinded-fable
187	
188	     The third push keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
189	- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
190	- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and say so in your report.
191	# The report and the record
192	
193	## What every report holds
194	
195	Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.
196	
197	A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.
198	
199	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
200	
201	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
202	
203	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
204	
205	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
206	- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
207	- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
208	- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
209	- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
210	- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
211	- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.
212	
213	## At a point to report
214	
215	- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
216	- Then finish the work.
217	- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
218	
219	## Timings and citations
220	
221	- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
222	- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
223	- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
224	- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.
225	
226	## POSITIONS and FACTS
227	
228	POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.
229	
230	Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".
231	
232	## The gap ledger
233	
234	The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).
235	
236	A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.
237	
238	- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
239	- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
240	- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.
241	
242	Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.
243	
244	A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.
245	
246	The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.
247	
248	## Reading the record
249	
250	Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:
251	
252	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh
253	
254	- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
255	- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
256	- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
257	- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
258	- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
259	- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
260	- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
261	- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.
262	
263	A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.
264	
265	Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:
266	
267	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE
268	
269	## Writing to the record
270	
271	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
272	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
273	- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
274	  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
275	  - what it means for the work;
276	  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
277	  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
278	  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
279	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
280	- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
281	- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.
282	
283	Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.
284	
285	    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"
286	
287	To add a row:
288	
289	1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
290	2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
291	3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.
292	
293	To change a row:
294	
295	- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters.
296	- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
297	- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
298	- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
299	- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.
300	
301	## The repository's history
302	
303	- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
304	- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
305	- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
306	- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
307	- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
308	- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.
309	# The specification
310	
311	Three folders hold the team's specification:
312	
313	- `Specification/` is the team's text, as the revival revises it. It says what the language means, except where a decision of the curator says otherwise.
314	- `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the unrevised copy. Cite it as "the Working Draft of February 2011". Only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Leave this copy unchanged.
315	- `Documentation/Specification/` is the team's later restart, which they did not finish. If its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, cite it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word.
316	
317	Appendix I, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, records the changes to the text. Its revival section has one entry for each change that the revival made.
318	
319	A draft build prints the team's `\note{}` boxes, and a release build hides them. Many say that a feature was not built, for example "Reduction variables are not yet supported." Before you record a missing feature as a gap, grep the notes of its chapter: `grep -n '\\note{' Specification/<file>.tex`.
320	
321	The api listings of the library part are generated from the library's `.fsi` files when the specification is built (`Specification/library/apis/`, not in the tree). A listing shows the library itself, so it cannot justify a change of the library. Cite the `.fsi` file.
322	
323	To weigh the specification against the team's later texts, or to find the designers' reason for a rule, read `exploring.md`, "Weighing the sources".
324	
325	## Changing the text: the revision form
326	
327	Every change of the text has the four parts below, so that no disagreement between the text and an implementation stays hidden.
328	
329	1. An entry in the revival section of Appendix I: a `\subsection` with a `\seclabel`. The entry gives:
330	   - the affected sections, the change, its rationale and its effect. The effect names each departure: each way in which walk or the compiled path does not do what the new text says, with its ledger row.
331	   - the original text, quoted with its path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`;
332	   - what a reversal to the alternative not taken would need;
333	   - the decision of the curator that it follows (its POSITIONS entry), or the reason that your brief gives.
334	
335	   For the form, print one entry, about 2 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:Specification/appendices/changes.tex#choice of a coercion'`.
336	
337	2. At each changed passage, a callout that prints in every build, unlike a `\note`:
338	
339	       \revision{<label>}{<what changed, in a sentence or two>}
340	
341	   `<label>` is the `\seclabel` of the entry. `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex` defines `\revision`.
342	
343	3. The front matter's one paragraph on the revision, in `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex`. If your change makes it false, correct it.
344	
345	4. The full reasoning, in `decision-record.md` in the folder of your work under `explorations/`: each changed passage, the original and the new text, the reason, and the way back. For the form, print one passage of an earlier record, about 4 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md#3.3'`.
346	
347	If the revision refuses an example, keep the example in the text, marked "Not allowed", as the specification itself does. If your change contradicts a calculus of Appendix A, keep the calculus's rules and soundness claims. Add a callout to it that says what it predates.
348	
349	Check each changed sentence of `Specification/` or `Documentation/` against the curator's decisions. If it says what walk or the compiled path does, run a program that shows it.
350	
351	## Building it
352	
353	To check your LaTeX, build the specification in a built tree, after the setup lines. It takes about 90 s, so start it detached (`session.md`, "Long commands"):
354	
355	    nohup bash -c '( cd Specification/fortress && ./ant genSource && ./ant tex ) > tmp/spec.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/spec.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &
356	
357	- Both commands must end in `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, and `grep -c 'Reference .* undefined\|multiply defined\|Undefined control sequence' Specification/fortress/fortress.log` must print 0.
358	- If `pdflatex` is missing, install the packages of the `PKGS` line of `explorations/experiment/setup.sh` with `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y`.
359	- The build writes only ignored files, its log among them, which can reach 400 MB. Remove them afterwards: `git clean -fXq -- Specification`.
360	- Update `Specification/fortress.pdf` only if your brief asks for it: copy `Specification/fortress/fortress.pdf` over it.
361	
362	## When the text and an implementation disagree
363	
364	- If a decision of the curator says which side is correct, the other side is wrong. If the wrong side is in your area, change it to agree. If not, record the departure as `tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", says.
365	- If no decision says so, the disagreement is a conflict. Switch to exploring (`exploring.md`).
366	- If the passage has an Appendix I entry, name the departure or the conflict in the entry's effect, with its ledger row. Then the text claims no more than holds.
367	
368	## Citing it
369	
370	- If your change renames or removes a section that a test names, update that citation in the same commit.
371	- Inside the text, cite a section with `\secref{label}`.
372

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:66
- P-155 **The compiled checker checks the overloads of symbolic operators before the switch-over.** Today its overloading check reads an operator only if its name is a word of capitals, such as `MAX`, so `+`, `^`, `||`, the subscripts and the other symbolic operators pass unchecked. The check must read them by the rules that it applies to any function, so that the distance to the switch-over reaches zero with them checked. Why: the skip is a gap that the team knew, not a rule: the specification's appendix of proposed features calls the library's two subscript operators "not really a valid overloading" (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:186-207`, its item on array indexing). A zero with them unchecked would hide known errors. Each design that the check needs is brought to the curator before its rung, with the probe's measurement (`perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2/REPORT.md`); the two it found are decided: P-156, the subscripts' index bound, and P-157, vectors that stay additive groups by a change to the checker's exclusion test. Row 584: the check and its rungs.

POSITIONS.md:61
- P-148 **The checker's speed comes right after its correctness in priority: a rung that changes the compiled checker also makes the change fast.** The rung times the checker before and after its change. It first makes the change correct. Then, in the same rung, it makes the new code fast, without changing which programs the checker accepts or refuses. So no optimization is left to be done by hand after the landing. Why: the checker must stay usable as it grows. Some slowdown is fine, but new checks have made it orders of magnitude slower, so that the checker ran past the time limit of the batch gate's count stage, and rungs could not land. The timing is a smoke test: one run of each tree, to catch a slowdown of several times; a small difference is noise. The `fortress-repo` skill (`compiler.md`, "The checker's time") gives the steps, their commands and what the rung reports.

# Climb batch 21b, rung C (rung-symbolic-check): record lines

## Findings

1. **The compiled checker's overloading check reads every operator.** Its top-level loop, its trait check's provided methods and its overriding return types now read `isCheckedName`, which admits every `SOp` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala:270`, `:396`, `:405`, `:766-773`). `isDeclaredName`, which the export check reads (`ExportChecker.scala:275`), is unchanged, so row 782 stays latent.
   - Conditions: wip/rung-symbolic-check at `ed4782762` (code of `4fb3242fa`), on climb batch 21's landed library.
   - Evidence, the distance stage (`explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh`): '#total 5', 'typecheck 4', 'export 1', '#crash none'. `compare.sh` against climb batch 21's gate: 'DISTANCE SAME   5'. The five rows equal `explorations/compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv` row by row, the export error's 43 entries included.
   - Evidence, against the base's full check (`plan-21/probes/full-check-base.tsv`): 'landed 191 now 5', none come.
   - Evidence, the count stage: '#total 3', the landed table byte for byte.
   - Evidence, the tests: `XXXSymbolicOperatorOverloadUnrelated` ('Invalid overloading of + in component ...') and `XXXFunctionalMethodMeetOperatorChecker` ('Invalid overloading of || in object Vo'); both compile on the base.
   - What it means: P-155's zero is now measured with every operator checked. The stock stages are the full check, so run 1's 186 cleared sites are held by gated stages, and fork 34's fallback is not needed.
2. **The crash on a `where`-clause comprises trait's self type** (NEW-C-1). Outside the trait, `removeSelf` read `self`'s type `AnyC & C[\E\]` with `E` unbound. `checkCC` and `checkP` then reached `staticParam(E)`, 'E is not in the kind env'. It did so on three paths: the overloading check's top-level set (`toFunctionArrows`'s `equiv`), a call from outside (`CoercionOracle.moreSpecific`), and rung X's bounds reading in the exclusion test (`TypeSchemaAnalyzer.withBounds` from `meetEmptyWithBounds`). Rung X's exclusion arrows were not a path: a trait with a `comprises` clause keeps none.
   - The repair: `TypeAnalyzer.selfComprised` (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:604-622`), read by `removeSelf` (`:579`) and `withBounds` (`TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala:470-471`). It reads no listed type where the trait's `where`-clause variable is unbound in the kind environment, and the lookup counts as a read of the context. Inside the trait the variable is bound, so the body's reading is unchanged.
   - Evidence: `ComprisesWhereFunctionalMethodChecker` (typecheck, with a call) and `XXXComprisesWhereFunctionalMethodBounds`, both 'E is not in the kind env' on the base. On the distance stage, the three units' `||` checks (`List`'s api and component, `String`'s component) run with no crash line and no error.
   - What it means: `AnyList`'s `||` is checked.
3. **Row 775's program is cleared by the same repair.** The shape is a generic trait whose `comprises` clause lists `S[\E, F\]` at a `where`-clause `F` and overrides an inherited method. A dotted override gave 'F is not in the kind env [E -> KindBinding(E,E extends Object)][][]' on the old code, and a functional one 'F is not in the kind env [E$2 ...][T$1 ...][][]'. Both typecheck now.
   - Test: `ComprisesWhereOverrideChecker`, red on the old code through `old-fortress.sh junit`.
4. **The double count** (NEW-C-2). `checkOverloading`'s on-demand import loops added `getFunctions(index, f)` once for each name of the api with the operator's text. So an api with a prefix and an infix `-` added its `-` twice, and the duplicate check refused each declaration against itself. With the full check and no repair, the compiler's prelude refuses itself (CLIMB-BATCH-21.md, section 4).
   - Repair: `importsOnDemand` (`OverloadingChecker.scala:248-256`), once per api, at all three loops (`:291`, `:318`, `:349`).
   - Evidence: the guard `OperatorPrefixInfixImport` passes on the base and after. Under the loops-only checker (scratch classes) it is refused: 'There are multiple declarations of - with the same parameter type: (OperatorPrefixInfixApi.Pt, OperatorPrefixInfixApi.Pt)'. With the repair, the prelude's library order compiles all five jars.
5. **The ignored `except` clause** (NEW-C-3). The three loops tested `excepts.contains((m:IdOrOp) => m.getText.equals(text))`, which is always false. So a name that an on-demand import's `except` leaves out was still read, by identifiers on the base too.
   - Repair: in `importsOnDemand`.
   - Evidence: `ImportExceptOverload` and `ImportExceptByName`, 'There are multiple declarations of pick with the same parameter type: ImportExceptOverloadApi.P' on the base; both link and run PASS after; walk runs both.
   - Conditions: no component of the stages has an `except` clause, so the stages cannot move by it.
6. **The prelude's range `=`** (fork 15). `GeneratorZZ32` extends `Equality[\GeneratorZZ32\]` and also excludes `Number`, `Character` and `String` (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi:111`, `.fss:301`). The always-false top-level `=` is gone (formerly `.fsi:129`, `.fss:314`).
   - Evidence: compiled, `r = r` was false on the old code and is true now; `(1:3) = (1#3)` and `(2:4) = (2:5)` are false on both. `RangeEqRungJLink` links, and `XXXRangeEqRungJ` stays an expected failure ('FAIL:  ranges.tex, section "Ranges"').
7. **Row 726's test, respelled.** `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositionsOperator` now expects the checker's 'There are multiple declarations of ||'. It was 'Saw expected failure' on the code generator's message on the base, then red with the new key on the base, then 'Saw expected failure' after.
8. **The checker's time** (P-148). Machine: nproc 4, Intel Xeon @ 2.10 GHz, openjdk 25.0.4.1, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`.
   - The count stage: base 120.2 s (load 6.88), change 107.5 s (6.77), pass 94.3 s (1.83); a later pair, base 84.4 s (0.24) and pass 96.8 s (0.85).
   - The tables and the `run.txt` files are equal across base, change and pass.
   - JFR: the apis' overloading check took 2,838 of 6,125 samples on the base and 3,689 of 6,845 on the change. The growth is the exclusion test (814 to 1,296) and the Return Type Rule (948 to 1,212); the new code itself takes 0 to 22 samples.
   - The pass (`4fb3242fa`) tests `functionalMethodsAtOnePosition` first, which takes the specificity samples in `validOverloadingInner` from 379 to 302.
   - The distance stage took 256 s (FortressLibrary 190 s) at load 2.87, against 206 s at the last gate. This is one run, not a pair.
9. **No ladder file or microGPT component moved.** In a subset of 120 files, the 85 that the gate holds are at the same phases as climb batch 21's ladder. Three UP against the baseline (`NatReflectTest`, `genericTest1`, `genericTest2`) behave the same on the old code. The eighteen microGPT components are at the same phases.
10. **`ant testQuick` on the change**: 'Tests run: 1303, Failures: 0', 86, 263, 'BUILD SUCCESSFUL'. One more test, `XXXFunctionalMethodMeetOperatorChecker`, came after it, so the gate's compiler track should count 1,304.
11. **Walk's comment is now stale.** `OverloadedFunction.java:1894-1895` says walk's Meet Rule check reads "those the compiled checker checks (OverloadingChecker.isDeclaredName)". The compiled check now reads every operator, while walk's `checkedName` (`:1990-1994`) still reads `NodeUtil.validOp`. It is walk's file, which this rung does not edit.

## Revival change

**The change.**

The team's proposed-features appendix calls the library's two subscript operators "not really a valid overloading" (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:186-207`). The code generator's own message names the static analysis as at fault.

- **An api is read once, and its except clause is read.** The team's checker read an api's declarations once for each of its names whose text was the operator's, so twice for an api with a prefix and an infix `-`.   - Reason: a name is imported on demand only if it is "neither listed in the except clause nor explicitly imported", and the overloading rules apply to the declarations "declared or imported" (`Specification/basic/components/source-code.tex:248-258`). With every operator checked, the team's code refuses the compiler's prelude itself, 'There are multiple declarations of - with the same parameter type: (ZZ, ZZ)', each declaration against itself.
- **A self type is read as its trait outside the trait.** The team's analyzer read a trait's self type, the trait met with the types its `comprises` clause lists, with those types as written (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:473-481` at `a874948ac`). Taking the `=` out alone leaves ranges with no `=`, '(ZZ32, ZZ32)->Boolean is not applicable to an argument of type (Range, Range).'

An ``ordinary'' operator (i.e., operators other than
 enclosing or vertical-line operators)
is a single token, and it is imported simply by putting \KWD{opr}
before it in the import statement.  This imports all of its prefix, postfix,
infix, multifix and nofix declarations.
A matched pair of enclosing operators is written \KWD{opr}
the left encloser, the right encloser, with \EXP{\cdot}
optionally between the two enclosers.
A vertical-line operator may be imported either as an infix operator or
a bracketing operator, according to the rules above for ordinary and
enclosing operators respectively.

An import-unqualified
statement may include an alias for each name it specifies.
%import APIName.{ name as name' (, name)^+ }
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{import}\:\TYP{APIName}.\{\,\VAR{name} \KWD{as}\:\VAR{name}' (, \VAR{name})^+\,\}\)
\end{Fortress}
In this case, the alias (unqualified) must be used
instead of the name declared by the actual imported declaration,
and the restriction about declarations
in the importing component or API
and names specified in other import-unqualified
statements
applies to the alias rather than the specified name.

For convenience, an on-demand import statement
allows all names declared by imported declarations
of the specified \apiN\ to be referred to with unqualified names:
%import APIName.{...}
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{import}\:\TYP{APIName}.\{\ldots\}\)
\end{Fortress}
This form permits an \KWD{except} clause,
which lists names that are \emph{not} permitted to be used unqualified
by that import-unqualified
statement
(it may be permitted by a declaration
in the importing component or API,
or by some other import-unqualified
statement).
%import APIName.{...} except { name (, name)^+ }
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{import}\:\TYP{APIName}.\{\ldots\} \KWD{except} \{\,\VAR{name} (, \VAR{name})^+\,\}\)
\end{Fortress}
A name \VAR{name} is imported on demand in a component \VAR{C}
from an API \VAR{A} only if all the following conditions hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \VAR{C} contains an on-demand import statement.
\item \VAR{name} is neither listed in the \KWD{except} clause
nor explicitly imported by \VAR{C}.
\item Either 1) a top-level or functional method declaration of \VAR{name}
appears in \VAR{C} or 2) a reference to \VAR{name} appears in component \VAR{C}
and \VAR{C} does not provide an explicit declaration of \VAR{name}.
\end{enumerate}

The set of all declarations that are declared or imported
(either explicitly or on demand) by a component must satisfy the overloading
rules (and in particular, any nonfunctional declaration must not be overloaded).
In addition, it is a static error if in a set of overloaded declarations,
any of the following are true:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Any declaration imported on demand is more specific than any explicit declaration.
\item Any top-level function declaration is more specific than any functional method declaration.
(This rule actually applies to declarations in a single component as well.)
\item
Any top-level function declaration imported on demand is more specific than any other declaration not in the same API as the top-level function declaration.
\end{enumerate}
It is also a static error to explicitly import a name from an API
that does not declare it, or to have multiple import-on-demand statements
with the same API.

If there is no imported declaration matching a reference, it is a static error.
If there is more than one imported declaration that a reference may refer to,
it is a static error.

#!/bin/bash
# The gate's checker-count stage: run the bytecode compiler's static checker over the
# INTERPRETER's library, with the interpreter's prelude in scope, and print the per-api
# error table, the total and the crash line that follows it.
#
# Why it exists: POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-21, "the library route" - one library, the
# interpreter's, becomes the library the compiler checks - and step 1 of
# coordinator/library-route-judgement.md, which makes the distance to that goal a
# permanent gate stage rather than a one-off script. A change in the count is reported, not red (checker-gate-review.md).
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh sourced, after ant compileAll:
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir]
#
# It writes the table to <out-file> and prints it. Nothing in the tree is touched:
# javac output and the checker's caches go to the scratch directory (default: $TMPDIR
# or /tmp), and the caches are given to the JVM as -Dfortress.caches, honoured through
# ProjectProperties.java:261-269,283, so default_repository/ is never read or written.
# Exit 0 if the table holds a total; 1 if no table could be produced, or if the table holds
# no total because the run's errors are not the checker's (#stopped, below). 20 s in the
# main tree, measured 2026-09-22; it needs no library rebuild and no warm cache.
#
# The two sources beside this script are copies, taken 2026-09-22 from
# explorations/perf-probes/prelude/, so that the gate does not depend on a probe
# directory: WorldFlip.java (Shell.useInterpreterLibraries() plus
# PhaseOrder.compilerPhaseOrder, both public, which is the world switch without an edit
# to a tracked file) and shadow-src/.../StaticChecker.java, a copy of
# ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java with three
# instrumentation points added: it names each compilation unit it checks and prints that
# unit's error count, and it catches the OverloadingChecker crash instead of dying on it.
# It is put AHEAD of ProjectFortress/build on the classpath, the technique of
# perf-probes/prelude/run-all.sh:33-35. A copy of a tracked source goes stale silently,
# so the checksum of the tracked one is recorded here and the table's "#shadow" line
# says whether it still matches.
#
